1. Plan: break the request into work per discipline, in order (design, then assets and code, then the level, then
   tests). A small request may need one specialist; a one-line change you can make yourself.

name: delegation
description: Handing work to sub-agents with the delegate tool. Writing briefs, running sub-agents side by side, checking their work, and keeping the user as involved as they want. Use whenever you delegate.
---
# Delegating

`delegate` starts a sub-agent: a new session of another agent type, working in your worktree. It waits until the
sub-agent finishes and returns its last message, its report. The user sees it under your session and can talk to it.

## Briefs
The sub-agent starts with nothing but your brief. Include:
- the goal and what done looks like (files, names, sizes, behaviour);
- the context it needs: the design doc to read, the style, related assets and code, paths;
- constraints: what not to touch, conventions to follow;
- how involved the user wants to be: "ask the user before choosing a concept" or "choose yourself";
- what to report back: paths, decisions, open questions.

Give it a short `title`, which names its session.

## Side by side
Independent tasks can run at once: several `delegate` calls in one codemode script.

```js
const [model, sound] = await Promise.all([
  tools.delegate({ agentType: "art-director", title: "Treasure map model", task: "…" }),
  tools.delegate({ agentType: "audio-director", title: "Map pickup sound", task: "…" }),
]);
return [model, sound].join("\n\n---\n\n");
```

Dependent tasks go one after another (the model before the code that spawns it). GPU generation runs one job at a
time, so several art tasks queue rather than finishing sooner.

## Checking
Read the report, then check the work itself: the files, previews, `./build.sh test`. If it falls short, delegate
again with exactly what to fix. The new sub-agent doesn't see the old one's conversation: say what exists and
what's wrong.

## The user
The user decides how involved they are. Pass their preference on in every brief. When a choice is theirs (a
concept, a theme, a layout), the sub-agent asks with `ask_user`: the question shows in its session, and you wait.

# Goblin Gold

> The design overview: what the game is and what it's trying to be. Demo Game is the sandbox Game Studio is
> developed against, so this game stays deliberately small: big enough to show every studio module working
> together, small enough to change in an afternoon.

## Pitch
A small goblin wanders a mossy clearing looking for treasure. Walk up to a chest, open it, and celebrate the
gold inside. Find every chest to win.

## Pillars
- **Readable at a glance.** Chunky, stylised models and a calm palette; the goblin is always the clearest thing on screen.
- **Every action has a reaction.** Walking animates, chests creak open, the goblin waves when it finds gold.
- **Made in the studio.** Every asset comes from a Game Studio module (models from 3D Models, code from Game
  Code sessions), so the game doubles as a showcase of the pipeline.

## Core loop
1. Explore the clearing with **WASD** (hold the right mouse button and drag to turn the camera, wheel to zoom).
2. Near a closed chest, press **E** to open it: the lid swings open, gold is added to the counter and the goblin waves.
3. When every chest is open, the clearing is cleared.

## World
| Thing | Model | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Goblin (player) | `assets/models/goblin` | 1.1 m tall, rigged; clips `idle`, `walk`, `wave` |
| Treasure chest | `assets/models/chest` | 0.6 m; hinge rig with `open`/`close` clips; holds gold |
| Barrel | `assets/models/barrel` | 0.9 m scenery, solid |
| Boulder | `assets/models/rock` | 0.7 m mossy scenery, solid |

The clearing is `assets/scenes/clearing.json`: a grassy ground, four chests, and barrels and boulders placed
as landmarks. Each kind of thing is a prefab in `assets/prefabs/`.

## Music
| Piece | Score | Where it plays |
|---|---|---|
| Goblin Gold | `assets/music/goblin-gold/song.json` | The whole game, looping: D dorian, 104 bpm, flute and clarinet over pizzicato strings, about a minute |
| Treasure Found | `assets/music/treasure-found/song.json` | Once, when a chest opens: a glockenspiel flourish ending on D major |

## Scope
Single player, one scene, a few minutes of play. Deliberately left out: enemies, inventory, saving, sound effects (until the SFX module exists), menus beyond a "cleared" banner.

### Built-in components

| Component | Purpose | Key fields (zero = default) |
|---|---|---|
| `Name` | Display name, used by `find` and tools | (a string) |
| `Transform` | Position, rotation, scale relative to `parent` | `position`, `rotation` (identity), `scale` (1), `parent` |
| `Camera` | Renders from its entity looking along +Z; highest `priority` wins | `fov` (60), `near` (0.1), `far` (1000), `projection`, `ortho_size` |
| `Mesh_Renderer` | Draws a built-in shape or model file | `mesh`, `material`, `no_shadow`, `hidden` |
| `Light` | Point, directional (sun) or spot light along +Z | `kind` (Point), `color` (white), `intensity` (1), `range` (10), `spot_angle` (45), `shadows` |
| `Rigid_Body` | Physics body with one shape, auto-fitted to the mesh | `kind` (Static), `shape` (Box), `size`/`radius`/`height`, `density`, `friction`, `restitution`, `sensor`, `layer`, `mask` |
| `Character_Controller` | Walking capsule (feet at origin): slides, climbs slopes, pushes crates | `radius` (0.4), `height` (1.8), `velocity`, `grounded` (output) |
| `Animator` | Plays a skeletal clip from the entity's model, crossfading on change | `clip`, `speed` (1), `time`, `once`, `paused`, `fade` (0.2), `finished` (output) |
| `Audio_Source` | Positional sound on an entity | `sound`, `volume`, `pitch`, `loop`, `autoplay`, `non_spatial`, `min_distance`, `max_distance` |
| `Audio_Listener` | Where audio is heard from (default: the camera) | |
| `Particle_Emitter` | Billboard particles | `rate` (20/s), `burst`, `lifetime`, `speed`, `spread`, `gravity`, `size`, `color`, `additive`, `disabled` |
| `Lifetime` | Destroys the entity after `seconds` | `seconds` |
| `Net_Entity` | Replicates the entity in multiplayer | `id`, `owner`, `prefab` (set by `net_spawn`) |

Built-in meshes: `cube` (1 m), `sphere` (1 m diameter), `plane` (1×1 m, facing up), `cylinder`
(1 m diameter, 1 m tall), `capsule` (1 m diameter, 2 m tall), `cone`, `torus`. All are centred on the
origin. Model files: `.glb`/`.gltf` (with skeletal animation), `.obj`, `.iqm`, `.m3d`, `.vox`. Each mesh
can have at most **65,535 vertices** (raylib uses 16-bit indices). Larger meshes load but render corrupted,
and the engine logs an error naming the mesh. When exporting from Blender, clear custom split normals first,
or the glTF exporter splits every vertex per triangle corner.

`Material` overrides: `color` (tint), `texture` (albedo), `normal_map` (tangent space, +Y up as in glTF),
`roughness_map` (red channel, absolute unless `roughness` scales it), `uv_scale` (tiling), `metallic`, `roughness`,
`emissive` (linear RGB, can exceed 1 for glow), `transparent` (alpha blend), `unlit`. Built-in meshes have tangents
and 0..1 UVs per face, so a tiling surface is a plane with `uv_scale` = its size / the tile size:

```json
{"Mesh_Renderer": {"mesh": "plane", "material": {"texture": "textures/grass/grass.png", "normal_map": "textures/grass/grass_normal.png",
  "roughness_map": "textures/grass/grass_roughness.png", "uv_scale": [20, 20]}}}
```

---
name: texture-art
description: Game Studio's tileable surface textures (assets/textures/<name>/): prompting in the game's style, judging seamless candidates from their tiled previews, tile sizes in metres, normal and roughness maps, and how scenes use them. Use whenever making or changing a texture.
---
# Tileable surface textures

A texture is a folder `assets/textures/<name>/` (lower-kebab-case; "/" for folders, e.g. `ground/grass`):

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `texture.json` | The asset: `notes`, `prompt`, `tile` (metres per repeat), `source` (the chosen candidate), `normal_strength` (0-20, default 4), `roughness` ([min, max], default [0.55, 0.95]) |
| `candidates/<name>-<seed>-roll.png`, `-quilt.png` | Generated seamless candidates, two per seed; `candidates.json` records how each was made |
| `<name>.png`, `<name>_normal.png`, `<name>_roughness.png` | What scenes use: colour, normal (tangent space, +Y up), roughness. Written by `make_texture`: never edit them |

## Making one
1. **Prompt the surface and the game's style.** The studio adds "seamless, top-down, flat lighting"; you add what the
   surface is and the art direction from `docs/design/`. Without the style, surfaces come out photoreal: "short grass
   with small clover leaves, **stylised hand-painted game texture, calm palette**". Describe the material, not a scene
   (no horizon, objects or lighting).
2. `generate_texture` (2 seeds = 4 candidates, ~25 s a seed on the GPU). The sheet shows each candidate **tiled 2x2**:
   the middle cross is where the edges meet.
3. **Judge the tilings, not the single images:**
   - a visible line or step down the middle cross: a seam. Reject
   - the same blotch, spot or swirl repeating in a grid: it will look like wallpaper at a distance. Reject or regenerate
   - shading, a light direction, perspective or a vignette: it won't tile believably. Regenerate with a plainer prompt
   - Either method can win: `roll` (seamless while generating) is usually better on stones and bricks, `quilt` (cut
     afterwards) on wood and organic surfaces. Regular rows (bricks, cobbles) are the hardest: generate more seeds.
4. `make_texture` with the chosen `source` and its `tile`, then check the preview (colour tiled, normal, roughness).
   Raise `normal_strength` for deep relief (cobbles 5-7), lower it for flat surfaces (painted plaster 1-2).

## Tile sizes
How wide one repeat is in the world. The texture must look right at that size next to a 1.1 m goblin: count the
features (stones, planks, clover leaves) across one image and size them realistically for the style.

| Surface | Typical `tile` |
|---|---|
| Grass, moss, dirt | 2-3 m |
| Cobblestone path | 1.5-2 m |
| Wooden planks | 1-2 m |
| Stone or brick wall | 2-3 m |

## In scenes
A Mesh_Renderer's material names the three files (paths as the engine loads them, from `assets/`) and how often it
repeats: `uv_scale` = the surface's size / `tile`. Built-in meshes have 0..1 UVs per face; a plane's one face spans
its x and z scale, so a 20 × 20 m ground with a 2 m texture is `[10, 10]`:

```json
{"Mesh_Renderer": {"mesh": "plane", "material": {"texture": "textures/grass/grass.png", "normal_map": "textures/grass/grass_normal.png",
  "roughness_map": "textures/grass/grass_roughness.png", "uv_scale": [10, 10]}}}
```

Drop the material's `color` when texturing (it tints the texture). People do the same with the Scenes inspector's
**Surface texture** picker, which computes `uv_scale` from the entity's size.
---
name: level-design
description: Editing headless-game-engine scenes and prefabs (assets/scenes/*.json, assets/prefabs/*.json) as Game Studio keeps them: the format, ids and prefab references, units and axes, placing models, and checking the result with preview_scene. Use whenever creating or changing a scene or prefab.
---
# Scenes and prefabs

A scene is `assets/scenes/<name>.json`; the game loads it by its path under `assets/` (`scenes/<name>.json`). A prefab
(`assets/prefabs/<name>.json`) has the same shape and its **first entity is the root**. The engine's reference is
"Scenes and prefabs" in `engine/docs/making-a-game.md`.

```json
{
  "notes": "Goblin Gold's clearing: the goblin starts in the middle, four chests to find.",
  "environment": {"sky_zenith": [0.25, 0.45, 0.75], "fog_density": 0.02},
  "entities": [
    {"id": 1, "Name": "Sun", "Transform": {"rotation": [50, 30, 0]}, "Light": {"kind": "Directional", "intensity": 1.3, "shadows": true}},
    {"id": 3, "Name": "Ground", "Transform": {"position": [0, -0.5, 0], "scale": [40, 1, 40]}, "Mesh_Renderer": {"mesh": "cube"}, "Rigid_Body": {}},
    {"id": 20, "prefab": "prefabs/chest.json", "Name": "Chest 1", "Transform": {"position": [4, 0, 6], "rotation": [0, 210, 0]}, "Chest": {"gold": 25}},
    {"id": 50, "Name": "Lantern", "notes": "Lights the path to chest 1", "Transform": {"position": [3, 0, 4.5]}, "Mesh_Renderer": {"mesh": "models/lantern/lantern.glb"}}
  ]
}
```

## Rules Game Studio relies on
- **Plain JSON**, one entity per line, as above. No comments: put them in `"notes"` (on the file or on an entity).
  The Scenes section rewrites files in this layout, so keep it to keep diffs small.
- **ids** are positive whole numbers, unique in the file, and **stable**: never renumber. New entities take an
  unused id (grouping by tens, as above, is fine). `Transform.parent` refers to a parent by its id.
- **Keep prefab instances as references**: `{"id": 21, "prefab": "prefabs/chest.json", "Transform": {...}}`. Any
  component written on the instance overrides the prefab root's, field by field. Don't copy a prefab's contents in.
- Every other key is a component name (`Name`, `Transform`, `Mesh_Renderer`, `Light`, `Rigid_Body`, the game's own,
  e.g. `Chest`). An unknown name or field is a warning in the engine's log; `preview_scene` reports them.
- Leave out fields at their default: zero means default for every engine field (`scale` omitted is 1).

## Units and axes
- Metres, degrees. **+Y up, +Z forward, -X right** (so +X is to the left when you look along +Z).
- `rotation` is `[pitch, yaw, roll]` in degrees; yaw turns around +Y. Models face +Z at yaw 0.
- Generated models (`assets/models/<name>/<name>.glb`) have their origin at the bottom centre, so `position.y = 0`
  stands them on flat ground at height 0. `model.json` next to each records its size.
- A model is placed with `Mesh_Renderer.mesh = "models/<name>/<name>.glb"`. Add `"Rigid_Body": {}` (static box
  around the mesh) when the player should bump into it; small decoration can do without.
- **A prefab instance gets all of the prefab's components, its `Rigid_Body` included**, at any scale: read the
  prefab before saying what an instance does. An instance can't drop a component, so anything the player should walk
  over (stepping stones, pebbles) places the model directly, with `Mesh_Renderer` and no `Rigid_Body`.

## Placement that reads well
- Leave walking room: about 1.5 m between things the player walks between; nothing inside anything else.
- Vary rotations and scales a little (yaw and 0.8-1.3) so repeated props don't look stamped.
- Group by purpose (props around a landmark), and keep the play area readable from the game's camera.

## Surfaces (textures)
Grounds, paths and floors are usually built-in planes with a texture from `assets/textures/` (made ones have
`<name>.png`, `_normal.png` and `_roughness.png`; `texture.json` says its `tile` in metres). Set the Mesh_Renderer's
material to the three files with `uv_scale` = the plane's x and z scale / `tile`, and drop its `color` (see the
**texture-art** skill for the format). A path or patch on the ground is a thinner plane 0.01-0.02 m above it, so the
two don't flicker. No texture for what you need? Ask the Art Director for one (`delegate`), with the surface and size.

## Check your work
`preview_scene` builds the game, opens the scene paused and returns screenshots: `top` (from above: +Z is up the
image, +X is to the left), `overview` (three-quarter, from the -Z side) and `game` (the scene's own Camera), or your own
`{position, target}` views. It also lists problems in the file and engine warnings. Call it **after the edit has
finished** (tools in one batch can run at the same time), and look at every image before saying it's done.
Include `game` in the last check: it's what the player sees.

Paused previews don't show what's solid. When the player should walk along or through something you placed, walk them
there: a scripted run (**engine-control** skill) that sets the player's Transform next to it, holds the move action
and asserts on the position. Keep the script in `build/` (`./build.sh test build/walk.jsonl`) so it isn't committed.
